First evening at Kenji’s
You walk into Kenji’s ramen bar in Madrid for the first time. Kenji only speaks Spanish with his customers. It is evening and you are hungry.
Ch. 5
Thank you too! See you tomorrow, Ana! Come back soon.
Hi! Good evening. Welcome.
Good evening!
Good morning!
In the evening you say “buenas noches”. “Buenos días” is only for the morning.
Good morning? It’s nine in the evening…
Goodbye!
“Adiós” means “goodbye”, not “hello”.
Leaving already? You’ve only just arrived!
I’m Kenji. What’s your name?
My name is Ana. Nice to meet you.
I’m twenty years old.
He asked your name, not your age: “Me llamo…”.
Very good… but what’s your name?
“¿Cómo te llamas?” = what’s your name, not “how are you”.
I’m glad. But I asked you your name.
Nice to meet you. What would you like to eat?
I’d like a ramen, please.
I’d like a bed, please.
“Cama” = bed. You meant “ramen”.
A bed? This is a restaurant, not a hotel.
I don’t like eating.
Order something: “Quiero…, por favor”.
Then why did you come to a restaurant?
Very good. And to drink? Water, tea or beer?
A green tea, please.
A bread, please.
He offered you water, tea or beer.
You don’t drink bread… Water, tea or beer?
Yes.
It was an either-or question: pick one.
Yes what? Water, tea or beer?
Here’s your ramen. Do you like it?
Yes, I like it a lot! It’s very good.
Yes, I like them a lot.
For one thing: “me gusta”. “Me gustan” is for several.
Them? It’s just one ramen…
I’m cold.
Answer the question: “Sí, me gusta”.
Well, the ramen is hot… Do you like it or not?
That’s twelve euros, please.
Here you are. Thanks, Kenji! See you tomorrow.
Pay and say goodbye: “Aquí tienes. Gracias”.
Thirty-five… but it’s twelve euros.
Good evening, my name is Ana.
We’ve already introduced ourselves. Now you pay.
Yes, I know, Ana. Twelve euros, please.
Lost in Madrid
You are in central Madrid and want to get to Puerta del Sol. Your phone is dead. An elderly lady is sitting on a bench.
Ch. 7
You’re welcome. Have a lovely day in Madrid!
Good afternoon. Do you need help?
Yes, please. Where is Puerta del Sol?
Yes, what time is it?
You are looking for a place: “¿Dónde está…?”.
It’s five o’clock. Anything else?
No, thank you. Where is the sun?
The place is called “la Puerta del Sol”, not just “el sol”.
The sun? Well… in the sky, dear.
It’s very close. Go straight ahead and turn left at the second street.
Straight ahead and left at the second street. Is it far?
Straight ahead and right at the first street.
“Izquierda” = left, “derecha” = right, “segunda” = second.
No, no. Left, at the second one.
Thanks, I’ll go by car.
Repeat the directions to make sure you understood.
By car? You haven’t got a car…
No, it’s a five-minute walk. There’s a statue with a bear.
Perfect! Thank you very much, madam.
A bear? How scary! I’m not going.
“Estatua” = statue. The bear at Sol is the symbol of Madrid.
It’s a statue, dear, it doesn’t bite.
You’re welcome.
“De nada” is the answer to “gracias”. Here you are the one thanking.
You’re welcome? I’m the one helping you…
The interview at the Cervantes
You are Ana, at the interview for a Spanish teaching job at the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest. The director, Mr Martínez, speaks formally (usted).
Ch. 53
I think that’s an excellent answer. Welcome to the Instituto Cervantes, madam.
Good morning, madam. Please take a seat. Why do you want to work with us?
Because I love teaching and I would like my students to discover Spanish culture.
(the same idea, with a mood mistake)
After “me gustaría que” comes the imperfect subjunctive: “descubrieran”.
Interesting… although a teacher ought to use the subjunctive correctly, don’t you think?
Because I need the money, to be honest.
In an interview, talk about your professional motivation.
I appreciate your honesty… but I was expecting a different answer.
I see you have a little girl. Could you work in the afternoons?
Yes, provided you let me know in advance, I could organise myself.
(with a mood mistake)
“Siempre que” = provided that → subjunctive: “me avisen”.
I get the idea… but conditional “siempre que” needs the subjunctive.
And what business is that of yours?
The question was about the schedule, not personal. Answer politely.
…Very well. Let’s move on to the next question.
Last question: if a student never did their homework, what would you do?
I would talk to them to understand what is going on and look for a way to motivate them.
(wrong tense)
To “si + imperfect subjunctive” you answer with the conditional: “hablaría”.
All right, but I asked what you would do, hypothetically.
I would throw them out of the class.
The grammar is fine, but the answer isn’t suitable for a teacher.
Hmm. I was expecting something more educational.
You are in Tokyo on your first day. You are looking for the station. You ask a young woman walking by.
Ch. 3
You’re welcome. Take care!
Yes, what’s the matter?
Excuse me. Where is the station?
What is the station?
“Where” is どこ, not なん (what).
The station is… a station.
Nice to meet you. I’m the station.
That’s how you introduce yourself. To ask about a place: “～ は どこ です か”.
Sorry? You are the station?
The station is over there. It’s that white building.
Over there, yes. Does it have a toilet too?
Here?
ここ = here, あそこ = over there (far).
No, not here. Over there.
Is it a white cat?
たてもの = building.
A cat? No, it’s a building.
Yes, it’s inside the station.
Thank you very much!
Enjoy your meal! (before eating)
いただきます is said before eating. To say thank you: ありがとう ございます.
Sorry? There’s nothing to eat.
Sorry, I don’t understand.
なか = inside. The toilet is in the station.
In the station. Inside.
Ramen at Kenji’s (in Japanese)
Kenji suggests you practise Japanese: today he only speaks Japanese to you, as in a Tokyo noodle bar.
Ch. 6
Thank you very much! Please come again!
Welcome! How many are you?
One person (alone).
One (thing).
For people: ひとり, ふたり. ひとつ is for things.
One thing? You’re not a thing.
いただきます is said when the food is in front of you.
The ramen isn’t here yet!
This way, please. What would you like to eat?
A miso ramen, please.
(wrong particle)
With ください, the object takes を: ～を ください.
Yes… but you say “o kudasai”.
I drink ramen.
Ramen is eaten: たべます. のみます = to drink.
Drink it? Just the soup?
And to drink?
A tea, please.
I eat tea.
Tea is drunk: のみます. Or simply: おちゃ を おねがいします.
You eat tea? How unusual.
No, ramen.
のみもの = drink.
You’ve already ordered the ramen. To drink?
Thank you for waiting. Miso ramen. How is it?
It’s very tasty!
It’s very expensive!
He asked about the taste: おいしい.
Sorry… we haven’t talked about money yet.
It’s very quiet!
For food: おいしい (tasty), まずい (bad).
The place? Or the ramen?
Sakura is lost
Sakura calls you: she is lost in Madrid, near the bear statue in Puerta del Sol. You know the way to Kenji’s place. Explain it to her in Japanese.
Ch. 24
I can see the red lantern! Daddy! Thank you, Ana!
Hello! I’m lost… What should I do?
It’s all right. Where are you now?
It’s all right. What time is it?
Ask her where she is: どこ に いる?
It’s twelve… but that’s not what matters right now!
Cry, please.
Better calm her down: だいじょうぶ.
What?! I don’t want to cry!
I’m in front of the bear statue.
Then, if you go straight along the main street, you’ll come to a traffic light.
(wrong tense: “there was a traffic light”)
For directions: dictionary form + と, then the present: しんごう が ある.
“There was”? Isn’t it there any more?
The bear is dangerous! Run!
ぞう = statue. Give her directions: まっすぐ いく と…
It’s a statue… it doesn’t move.
I found the traffic light! And then?
Cross, turn left. At the third corner there’s a red lantern.
Eat the traffic light, turn left.
You cross the traffic light: わたる → わたって.
Eat the traffic light?! Impossible!
Turn right.
The place is on the left: ひだり.
Right? The card says left.
